posts.text:
Your company doesn't need to be your family.

Your coworkers don't need to be your best friends.

Your job doesn't need to be your passion.

And your manager doesn't need to believe in you.

It's okay to have a job that simply pays you well 
and gives you enough freedom to enjoy your actual life.

We've romanticized careers way too much.

Sometimes work is just work.

And that's not sad.

That's freedom.

Saw this on Reddit and it made me furious.

A job posting asking for 4+ years of LLM production experience.

ChatGPT launched back in November 2022.

Do the math.

4+ years for technology that has existed for less than 4 years.

This isn't a typo and it's not even about LLMs.

It's about how hiring managers copy-paste requirements from legacy job specs without thinking, slap AI on top, and call it a modern role.

It happens more than you think.

A lot of hiring managers still don't understand the tools they're hiring for.

Which means two things for you.

1. Don't disqualify yourself from roles because the requirements sound impossible. Read them critically. Many are written on autopilot.

2. The candidate who can walk into an interview and calmly explain what is actually realistic to build with LLMs right now. 

That person stands out immediately.

Domain knowledge plus clear thinking beats inflated credentials when the bar is set by someone who doesn't know what they're asking for.

Btw what is the most unrealistic job requirement you have seen recently?

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄?

Most people use Claude or ChatGPT like a search engine.

They ask, accept and move on with whatever the LLM provides.

In a real data workflow, you need to know:

→ Is this SQL query actually doing what I asked, or what it thinks I asked?

→ Is this code production-safe or just plausible-looking?

→ Is this analysis grounded in the data I provided or hallucinated?

→ When should I trust output and when should I verify line-by-line?


That's the sole reason I make my cohort members work through 4 real examples:

→ An AI-generated SQL query with a subtle JOIN bug
→ A data cleaning script that silently dropped 30% of rows
→ A chart suggestion that misrepresented the underlying distribution
→ A summary that confidently stated something the data didn't support

My students are often able to catch most of the issues. The ones they miss usually spark the best conversations of the session.

This is the kind of judgment that's becoming the actual differentiator in data work and it's almost impossible to learn from a tutorial.

If anyone wants me to break down one of these examples publicly, drop a comment below and I'll do it in a separate post.

𝐏.𝐒. If you're overwhelmed by all the conflicting advice about getting into Data & AI, check out www.datacareerschool.com

The fastest-rising salaries in data right now are in data engineering. 

Let me share why and what to learn first if you're considering the pivot:

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘀𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗴:

→ Every ML and AI initiative needs clean reliable data pipelines first

→ Most companies are 2-3 years behind on data infrastructure

→ The skillset blends software engineering and data. Fewer people have both skills

→ Cloud + modern data stack tools didn't exist 5 years ago so even senior people are still learning

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 (𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿):

1. Strong SQL: not surface-level but actually deep (window functions, CTEs, query optimization)

2. Python beyond pandas: file handling, APIs, error handling, basic OOP

3. Linux command line basics: bash, ssh, file permissions

4. Docker: every modern data role touches this

5. One orchestrator (Airflow or Prefect)

6. One transformation tool (dbt)

7. One cloud warehouse (BigQuery or Snowflake)

You don't need all of these on day one of a job search. 

The first 3 will get you interviews. The rest you can pick up on the job.

𝐏.𝐒. I help aspiring data professionals move beyond tutorials by building projects and portfolios that demonstrate real skills: www.datacareerschool.com

As a kid, I thought becoming an adult meant freedom.

Eat what you want.

Go where you want.

Buy what you want.

Turns out adulthood is mostly asking yourself questions like:

Do I really need this?

Can this wait until next month?

Why is there another subscription I forgot about?

Freedom is real.

But so are the bills.
